cues.en: So why would we use Sapper?
What does it bring to the svelte table?
Now, first of all, it's important to mention that Sapper is not an alternative to Svelte, but it
enhances it.
It enhances it with two main features, and that would be routing.
So the possibility to whilst still having a single page application support different URLs and rendering
different content onto the screen based on which your URL is visited still entirely in the browser,
but nonetheless with support for links and routes and so on.
And it also adds server side rendering.
Now as you learned, svelte runs in the browser.
It's JavaScript that runs in the browser and it updates the entire page in the browser.
And that is cool because that is pretty fast.
And when we click a button, things instantly change.
But when a page is first loaded, then this actually means that the page is downloaded, the JavaScript
is downloaded, and then the page has to be built on the client and that is where server side rendering
changes something.
It moves that initial first rendering onto a node JS server.
But let's start with routing.
It allows us to have multiple pages even in a single page application, as I mentioned, and Sapper
supports this or adds this feature by allowing us to map svelte components to URL paths so that you
can say if the user enters my domain.com slash about, then this svelte component should be rendered
on the screen.
Server side rendering can speed up the first render because it renders the page on the server and serves
the finished page to the client.
And thereafter this turns into a single page application on the client.
So the first page we ship is not an empty HTML file with a bunch of JavaScript, but actually populated
HTML file with less JavaScript and therefore the work is moved to the server, which can be useful if
our users have slower devices or if we have a very work intensive first render cycle.
And it also helps with search engine optimization because if a search engine crawler visits your page
and it sees an empty HTML page, it might not wait for your JavaScript code to render something meaningful
in the client.
If, on the other hand, you use server side rendering, then you do ship a populated page.
So a page with content and therefore search engine crawlers.
See what your users see.
So for users it might or might not make a difference depending on how long that initial render takes.
But for search engine crawlers.
Server side rendering will always be a bit better because they see what the user sees.
Of course, it's worth mentioning that not every page needs search engine optimization.
If you're building a page where users have to log in and then they navigate in their own dashboard,
that of course would be parts of an app that would never be indexed by a search engine.
And therefore there you might not need this.
If you're on the other hand, building a blog, then search engine optimization might be super important
and you definitely want to make sure that you always show the search engine crawler the finished content.
Now sapper here also ships with a built in server side pre-rendering setup for your svelte components.
So Sapper essentially is a tool you could say, or a framework that builds up on the svelte package,
which gives you everything you need to have a running NodeJS server which pre renders your svelte components
per request and which also adds routing to your svelte app so that you have a single page, svelte application
after that first load.
But that first load is pre rendered and in that single page application which you have thereafter,
you can go to different pages with URLs, something we couldn't do thus far in our meetup project.
For example there, if you remember that meetup detail page, if you want to call it page, it didn't
have a separate URL.
Instead we just clicked a button and loaded a new component, but the URL never changed.
And that of course means we never had an entry point that will lead directly to that page.
So what is Sapper, then?
Well, as I just mentioned.
Sapper builds up on Svelte.
You have your svelte app, which standalone just runs in the browser and you build your single page
application there with svelte components.
Sapper builds up on this and gives you a nodejs server which pre renders your svelte components and
in addition it gives you a server side rendering framework.
It gives you a structure, some ideas on how you should structure your app to also map certain svelte
components to certain paths in the URL.
And together you therefore get a pre rendered page on the first load and a single page application thereafter.
Now let's have a look at all of this in code.
